place-pktrm.title: Where the subway began
place-pktrm.body: Park Street opened on September 1, 1897 as part of the Tremont Street Subway, the first subway in the United States.

place-pktrm.title: Boston Common
place-pktrm.body: The station sits beneath Boston Common, established in 1634 and generally regarded as the oldest city park in the United States.

place-pktrm.title: Freedom Trail starts here
place-pktrm.body: The 2.5-mile Freedom Trail begins at Boston Common and passes the State House, Park Street Church and the Granary Burying Ground within a few blocks.

place-dwnxg.title: Old South Meeting House
place-dwnxg.body: The meeting that led to the Boston Tea Party began at Old South Meeting House on December 16, 1773, a short walk from this station.

place-dwnxg.title: A shopping crossroads
place-dwnxg.body: Downtown Crossing is a pedestrian shopping district where the Red and Orange lines cross.

place-dwnxg.title: Old Corner Bookstore
place-dwnxg.body: The Old Corner Bookstore, a Freedom Trail stop, was a 19th-century publishing house for authors like Hawthorne and Emerson.

place-gover.title: Boston City Hall
place-gover.body: Boston City Hall, a landmark of Brutalist architecture, opened in 1968 on the site of the former Scollay Square.

place-gover.title: King's Chapel
place-gover.body: King's Chapel, a few steps away, was founded in 1686 as the first Anglican church in New England; its granite building dates to the 1750s.

place-gover.title: Boston Latin School site
place-gover.body: A plaque and a statue of Benjamin Franklin outside Old City Hall mark the site of Boston Latin School, founded in 1635 and the oldest public school in the United States.

place-state.title: Old State House
place-state.body: Built in 1713, the Old State House is one of the oldest surviving public buildings in Boston. The Declaration of Independence was read from its balcony on July 18, 1776.

place-state.title: Boston Massacre
place-state.body: The Boston Massacre took place on March 5, 1770 at the spot now marked by a ring of cobblestones outside the Old State House.

place-state.title: Faneuil Hall
place-state.body: Faneuil Hall, opened in 1742, earned the nickname Cradle of Liberty as a meeting place for colonial protest.

place-haecl.title: Haymarket produce market
place-haecl.body: An open-air produce market sets up near the station on Fridays and Saturdays.

place-haecl.title: Union Oyster House
place-haecl.body: Union Oyster House, a few blocks away, has operated since 1826 and calls itself America's oldest continuously operating restaurant.

place-haecl.title: Paul Revere House
place-haecl.body: Built around 1680, the Paul Revere House is the oldest remaining building in downtown Boston.

place-north.title: TD Garden
place-north.body: TD Garden, home of the Bruins and the Celtics, sits directly above North Station.

place-north.title: Copp's Hill
place-north.body: Copp's Hill Burying Ground, established in 1659, is the second oldest burying ground in Boston.

place-north.title: USS Constitution
place-north.body: The USS Constitution, launched in 1797, is the oldest commissioned warship still afloat.

place-coecl.title: Boston Public Library
place-coecl.body: The Boston Public Library, founded in 1848, was the first large free municipal library in the United States. Its McKim Building faces Copley Square.

place-coecl.title: Trinity Church
place-coecl.body: Trinity Church, completed in 1877 and designed by H. H. Richardson, anchors Copley Square.

place-coecl.title: Marathon finish line
place-coecl.body: The Boston Marathon finishes on Boylston Street beside Copley Square.

place-harsq.title: Red Line to Cambridge
place-harsq.body: The Red Line reached Harvard Square in 1912 through a subway built under Massachusetts Avenue.

place-harsq.title: Oldest university
place-harsq.body: Harvard was founded in 1636 and is the oldest institution of higher learning in the United States.

place-kencl.title: Fenway Park
place-kencl.body: Fenway Park opened in 1912 and is the oldest ballpark still in use in Major League Baseball. It is a short walk from Kenmore.

place-kencl.title: Three branches
place-kencl.body: The Green Line B, C and D branches all pass through Kenmore.

place-sstat.title: A grand terminal
place-sstat.body: South Station opened in 1899 and was once the busiest railroad terminal in the world.

place-sstat.title: Red Line and rail hub
place-sstat.body: Today South Station connects the Red Line, the Silver Line, commuter rail and Amtrak.

place-bbsta.title: Land made from a bay
place-bbsta.body: Back Bay was filled in from tidal flats starting in 1857; the neighborhood is known for its preserved Victorian brownstones.

place-bbsta.title: Orange Line and Amtrak
place-bbsta.body: Back Bay station serves the Orange Line, commuter rail and Amtrak.

place-aqucl.title: New England Aquarium
place-aqucl.body: The New England Aquarium opened in 1969 next to the station on Central Wharf.

place-aqucl.title: Long Wharf
place-aqucl.body: Nearby Long Wharf was built starting in 1710 and once reached a third of a mile into Boston Harbor.

place-ccmnl.title: Battle of Bunker Hill
place-ccmnl.body: The Battle of Bunker Hill was fought on June 17, 1775 in Charlestown.

place-ccmnl.title: Bunker Hill Monument
place-ccmnl.body: The Bunker Hill Monument is a 221-foot granite obelisk with 294 steps to the top.
